rows.description: A teenager waves a hand to ask someone to step back or not crowd them. The same motion can mean stay away, not now, or give me air, and cultures differ on how blunt it is; a verbal follow-up clarifies without shaming the other person.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager raises a palm to stop a friend or sibling mid-rant, meaning I need a moment or I disagree. It can protect a boundary, but it can also read as dismissive; saying a few words like give me a second keeps the respect intact.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager finds that pointing with a whole hand, a chin or lips, or a thumb differs by region, and some styles feel rude elsewhere. A descriptive gesture can mislead, so pairing it with words and checking understanding helps.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager narrating a match or a prank sweeps hands to show speed, distance and drama. Expanded gestures usually signal excitement and involvement, while very small ones may suggest tiredness or reluctance; culture strongly shapes gesture size.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: sadness, excitement, tiredness

rows.description: A teenager preparing for an interview or public speaking practises standing straight and taking a breath, which can help nerves. Confidence also comes from preparation; exaggerated power poses do not replace real skill.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: relief from stress

rows.subtype: Slumping and crossing arms as protection [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager slumps, hunches or crosses arms in a tense home or crowd, often to feel smaller or safer. Arms crossed may mean cold, comfort or defence, so reading it as rudeness misses the mark; a chat about how they feel may help.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager dances in a group, at a wedding baraat, on a practice reel or at a school event to show joy and belonging. Styles vary by culture and gender norms; pressure to perform or teasing can turn joy into shame, so choice matters.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: joy, shame, nostalgia

rows.subtype: Walking away as boundary or avoidance [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager walks away from a fight, a taunt or a hard talk. It may be wise de-escalation, embarrassment or avoidance; saying I need a break and will come back makes the meaning clear and keeps trust.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager freezes, cannot speak or move when confronted, threatened or pressured. Freezing is a common involuntary stress response, not consent or agreement, and others should never read stillness as a yes.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Shielding the body and avoiding notice [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager pulls sleeves over hands, hunches or covers the face when embarrassed, self-conscious or uneasy around someone. It may signal shame or fear of being seen; steady acceptance helps, and fear of a particular person merits a trusted adult.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: fear, anxiety, shame, embarrassment
